lessons.title: The Marketing Mix and the Four Ps
lessons.description: How product, price, place and promotion work together to build a brand image.
lessons.content_html:
What Is the Marketing Mix?

A start-up can have a great product and still fail to sell it if the price is wrong, customers cannot find it, or nobody knows it exists. The marketing mix is the set of decisions that brings a product to market in a joined-up way. It is called “the four Ps” because each element starts with the letter P: Product, Price, Place and Promotion.

The four Ps are not independent of each other. They must work together to give a consistent message to the customer. A business that sets a high price but sells through a budget supermarket is sending mixed signals — and customers will be confused about whether the product is premium or economy. The extended-response evaluation question in the written exam always focuses on Topic Area 4 (marketing), and high-scoring answers show how the four Ps interact and reinforce each other.

Product

Product refers to what the business is selling and all the features that go with it: quality, design, features, packaging, brand name and after-sales service. A product does not have to be a physical object — it can be a service such as a haircut, a cleaning company or a web design agency. For a start-up, the key product decisions are: What exactly are we offering? What makes it different from what rivals sell? What quality level will we aim for?

Product quality shapes every other element of the mix. A high-quality, distinctive product (think of a handmade leather bag or a bespoke wedding cake) can support a higher price, exclusive place decisions and premium-feeling promotion. A functional, no-frills product sits better with economy pricing and wide, accessible distribution.

Price

Price is what the business charges customers for its product. It must cover costs and generate profit, but it also signals quality to the customer. There are four pricing strategies a small business typically uses:

  • competitive pricing — setting a price close to what rivals charge, used when the product is similar to what is already on the market and customers can easily compare.
  • Psychological pricing — setting a price just below a round number (for example, £9.99 rather than £10.00) to make the product feel cheaper than it is.
  • Price skimming — launching at a high price to maximise income from early buyers before reducing the price later, typically used when the product is new and innovative.
  • Penetration pricing — launching at a low price to attract customers quickly and build market share, accepting lower margins in the short term.

The pricing strategy must align with the product and its target market. Qualitative decisions about price strategy are what the exam tests — not specific numerical prices.

Key Fact

The four pricing strategies are: competitive (match rivals), psychological (just below a round number), price skimming (high at launch, reduce later) and penetration (low at launch to build share). Price signals quality — a premium price suggests a premium product, while an economy price signals value.

Place

Place is how and where customers can access the product. The two broad categories are:

  • Physical channels — selling from a shop, market stall, pop-up, trade fair or other face-to-face setting. Physical channels allow customers to see, touch or try the product before buying and can build trust through personal service.
  • Digital channels (e-commerce) — selling through a business’s own website, a marketplace such as an online craft platform, or social media stores. Digital channels remove geographical limits — a sole trader in a small town can sell to customers across the country from their spare bedroom.

Many start-ups use both: they sell at a local market on Saturdays and take online orders during the week. The choice of place must match the product and price. An artisan product positioned as exclusive should not be placed on a discount-retailer’s shelf — it would undermine the premium brand image.

Physical premises give visibility and allow customers to inspect the product, but they carry high fixed costs: rent, rates and utilities must be paid every month. Digital channels cost less to set up and maintain — a website or marketplace listing is far cheaper than a high-street shop — but they require the business to manage delivery, returns and customer trust without face-to-face contact. For most start-ups with limited capital, beginning online and adding physical presence later is a sensible low-risk approach.

Promotion

Promotion is everything the business does to communicate its product to potential customers and persuade them to buy. For start-ups with small budgets, promotion choices matter enormously — money spent on the wrong channel is wasted. Promotion will be covered in detail in the next lesson. For now, the key point is that promotion must be consistent with the rest of the mix: a premium product sold at a high price should be promoted through high-quality imagery and carefully chosen media, not through heavy discounting or cut-price deals.

How the Four Ps Create a Brand Image

When all four Ps align, they create a brand image. There are two broad ends of the spectrum:

  • Premium brand image: high-quality product, high price, exclusive or selective place (specialist retailers, own website only), sophisticated promotion. Every element signals “this is worth paying more for.”
  • Economy brand image: functional product, low price, wide and accessible place (available everywhere), promotion focused on value and deals. Every element signals “this is great value for money.”

Most start-ups do not aim for one extreme or the other — they position themselves somewhere on the spectrum. But the four Ps must still be consistent. A business offering artisan pottery at £45 a piece should not promote it with a “two for the price of one” deal — that damages the premium image it has worked to build.

Key Fact

The four Ps are interdependent: changing one forces a rethink of the others. If a start-up raises its price (moving towards premium), it must also ensure the product quality, place and promotion all support that premium positioning. A mismatch between the Ps confuses customers and undermines sales.

The extended-response evaluation question in the written exam always focuses on the marketing mix. To reach the top band, you must do three things: (1) explain how at least two of the Ps work together in the specific business scenario; (2) show awareness of the trade-offs involved in a change to the mix; (3) reach a supported overall judgement rather than simply listing pros and cons. Generic answers that name the four Ps but do not apply them to the scenario will not reach the top tier regardless of length.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The single biggest error on marketing mix questions is treating the four Ps as four separate boxes and writing about each in isolation. High-scoring answers show how a change to one P has a knock-on effect on at least one other P. For example: “Increasing the price to a premium level means the business must also ensure its product quality matches that price point, because customers paying more will have higher expectations — and if the product disappoints, they will not return.” On the extended-response evaluation question, use at least two P-links in your analysis, and finish with a supported judgement about which change to the mix would be most effective for the specific business in the scenario. Avoid ending your answer with a neutral summary that merely repeats what you have already said.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The marketing mix is the combination of product, price, place and promotion. All four elements must be consistent with each other and with the target market — a mismatch between the Ps confuses customers and damages sales.
  • Price signals quality: premium pricing requires a premium product, selective place and high-quality promotion. Economy pricing signals value and requires wide, accessible distribution. The four Ps together create a brand image.
  • Changing one P in the mix requires a rethink of the others. On evaluation questions, linking at least two Ps together in your analysis and applying them explicitly to the scenario is what separates top-band answers from mid-band answers.

Hawser & Loom is a small private limited company in Whitby making handwoven wool scarves. Each scarf is priced at £85. The owner sells exclusively through the business's own website and at two specialist lifestyle stores. She is considering dropping the price to £45 to attract more customers.

Analyse how reducing the price might affect Hawser & Loom's marketing mix.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Identifies at least two P-interactions clearly and with analytical chains. For example: the lower price conflicts with the premium product positioning (£85 signals quality and craftsmanship; dropping to £45 may cause customers to question whether the quality has declined). The place strategy (specialist stores) may no longer be appropriate if the brand is repositioned as a mid-range product — specialist stores typically require brands to maintain a premium image. Promotion may need to shift away from aspirational imagery towards value messaging. Demonstrates clear understanding that the Ps are interdependent and that a price change cannot be made in isolation. Reaches a supported conclusion.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one clear P-interaction with development and some application to Hawser & Loom. Analysis is present but may cover fewer Ps or lack full development.

Developing (2 marks): Identifies that reducing the price will affect other elements of the mix but the links are superficial or incomplete.

Emerging (1 mark): States that the price will fall with limited analysis of any knock-on effect.

practice_questions.text:
Crannock Provisions is a small sole trader in Truro run by its founder, Bea. Crannock makes artisan chilli sauces using locally sourced Cornish peppers. Bea currently sells her sauces at £6.50 a bottle, which is higher than most supermarket alternatives. She distributes through two local farm shops and her own Instagram page. Sales have been slow and Bea is considering whether to change her marketing mix.

Evaluate whether Crannock Provisions should reduce its price to £3.99 as a way of improving sales.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Evaluates both the potential benefits and the risks of the price reduction, with clear and specific reference to the scenario. Benefits: a lower price may attract price-sensitive customers who have not bought at £6.50; it could increase volume and help cover fixed costs; it may widen the target market beyond premium buyers. Risks: £3.99 is close to mass-market supermarket prices, which could undermine the artisan positioning (locally sourced Cornish peppers, farm shop distribution) that justifies a premium price; it may force a rethink of place (farm shops may not stock a £3.99 product alongside artisan goods) and promotion (Instagram content built around premium craft food); and it may not increase profit if margins are already thin at £6.50. Evaluative conclusion adds new thinking — for example, that Bea should first investigate whether her current customers are price-sensitive or value-driven, and consider improving promotion before cutting price, because the limited sales may reflect a reach problem rather than a price problem.

Secure (5–7 marks): Discusses both sides with some reference to the scenario and some integration of P-links. Conclusion is present but may repeat earlier points.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies advantages or disadvantages of reducing the price without full integration of the marketing mix. Limited scenario application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): States a preference with minimal justification. Little engagement with the specific scenario.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a new start-up selling eco-friendly cleaning products might choose penetration pricing rather than price skimming when it first enters the market.
practice_questions.marks: Penetration pricing involves launching at a low price to attract customers quickly and build market share. This suits a new eco-friendly cleaning product because the market is competitive — there are already many established brands — so a high skimming price would deter customers who do not yet know the product and have no reason to pay a premium. By entering at a low price, the start-up can encourage trial purchases, build a customer base, and generate word-of-mouth recommendation. Once customers are loyal and familiar with the product's quality, the price can be raised. Price skimming, by contrast, works best for genuinely innovative or unique products with no competition — which does not describe a market with many existing eco-cleaning brands. [1 mark per developed point up to 4 marks: (1) what penetration pricing is; (2) why competition makes a high launch price risky; (3) how a low price encourages trial and builds market share; (4) why skimming would be inappropriate in this context.]

lessons.title: Advertising, Sales Promotion and Public Relations
lessons.description: Advertising mediums, sales promotion techniques and PR methods for small businesses.
lessons.content_html:
Promotion in the Marketing Mix

Promotion is the fourth P in the marketing mix. It covers everything a business does to raise awareness of its products and encourage purchase. A common misconception is that promotion and advertising are the same thing. They are not: advertising is just one type of promotion. Promotion also includes sales promotion techniques and public relations. This lesson covers all three.

Advertising Mediums

An advertising medium is the channel through which an advert reaches its audience. Start-ups must choose mediums that match their budget, their target audience and their brand image. Advertising mediums split into two broad groups: traditional (non-digital) and digital.

Non-digital advertising mediums include:

  • Leaflets — low-cost printed flyers, posted through letterboxes or handed out at events. Useful for local businesses targeting a specific area.
  • Newspapers — local or national print advertising. A local fish-and-chip shop might advertise in the town’s weekly paper to reach nearby residents.
  • Magazines — specialist publications allow the business to reach a defined interest group. A small outdoor clothing brand might advertise in a hiking magazine to find customers who already love walking.
  • Radio — adverts on local radio stations reach a broad local audience during commuting hours.
  • Billboards — large outdoor displays in high-footfall areas such as roadsides or shopping centres, suitable for building brand awareness over time.
  • Cinema — adverts shown before films reach a captive audience and can be targeted by film genre and local cinema location.
  • TV adverts — television advertising gives a business wide reach and strong visual impact. It is traditionally expensive, but regional TV slots can be more accessible for a small business. TV adverts are a named medium in the specification, added to the list in 2025.
Key Fact

The seven non-digital advertising mediums are: leaflets, newspapers, magazines, radio, billboards, cinema and TV adverts. TV adverts are the most recent addition to the list. A start-up on a tight budget will typically start with leaflets or local newspapers, while TV advertising requires a significantly larger spend.

Digital Advertising Mediums

Digital channels allow start-ups to reach specific audiences at lower cost than most traditional mediums. The named digital advertising mediums are:

  • Social media — platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Facebook allow businesses to post content, run paid adverts and communicate directly with followers. There are two distinct types of social media post, and the specification requires you to know the difference:
    • Business-generated posts — content created and controlled by the business itself (a photo of a new product, an announcement of opening hours, a promotional offer).
    • Third-party-generated posts — content created by customers, bloggers or influencers about the business or its products. The business does not control these, but positive third-party posts can be highly persuasive because they are seen as independent opinions rather than paid advertising.
  • Social networks — broader networking platforms where businesses can create communities, run groups or participate in conversations relevant to their audience.
  • Websites — a business’s own website is a digital shopfront. Good search-engine visibility drives customers to it without the ongoing cost of paid adverts.
  • Online banners — paid display adverts that appear on websites, targeted to users based on their browsing interests.
  • SMS (text messages) — promotional texts sent directly to customers who have opted in, delivering offers or updates instantly.
  • Podcasts — a business can sponsor an existing podcast relevant to its target audience, or create its own branded podcast to build an engaged listener community.
  • Vlogs (video blogs) — video content, typically on platforms such as YouTube, allows a business or individual to demonstrate products, share behind-the-scenes content or build a following over time.

This distinction matters in the exam. A business-generated post is planned, written and published by the business — it is under the business’s control, can be timed and targeted, but customers may view it sceptically because it is obviously self-promotional. A third-party-generated post comes from a customer review, a blogger’s write-up or an influencer’s recommendation — the business does not control what is said, but positive third-party posts tend to be more trusted because they appear independent. A start-up encouraging customers to leave reviews or tag them on social media is leveraging third-party generation.

Sales Promotion Techniques

Sales promotion techniques are time-limited tactics used to stimulate sales quickly. Unlike advertising, which builds awareness over time, sales promotion is designed to get customers to buy now. The seven techniques you need to know are:

  • Discounts — reducing the price for a limited time (for example, “20% off this weekend only”). Effective for clearing stock or attracting price-sensitive customers.
  • Competitions — customers enter a prize draw when they buy. Creates excitement and encourages purchase without permanently reducing the price.
  • BOGOF (Buy One Get One Free) — a form of discount where two units are sold for the price of one, doubling the perceived value.
  • Point of sale displays — eye-catching promotional material at the checkout or near the product in a physical location, encouraging impulse buying.
  • Free gifts — a free item given with a purchase (for example, a free tote bag with a first order). Adds perceived value without reducing the main product’s price.
  • Loyalty schemes — customers earn points or stamps with each purchase that can be exchanged for discounts or free products, encouraging repeat business.
  • Sponsorship — a business provides financial or in-kind support to an event, organisation or individual in exchange for brand visibility. A local bakery sponsoring a community fun run gets its name on race bibs and banners.
Key Fact

The seven sales promotion techniques are: discounts, competitions, BOGOF, point of sale, free gifts, loyalty schemes and sponsorship. Short-term promotions can drive immediate sales, but using discounts too frequently may train customers to wait for a deal rather than paying full price — a risk for a start-up trying to build a premium image.

Public Relations for Small Businesses

Public relations (PR) is about building and maintaining a positive reputation through unpaid coverage. Unlike advertising, PR is not directly paid for — a business earns media attention by doing or creating something genuinely interesting or newsworthy. For a small start-up, PR can be a cost-effective way to reach audiences that paid advertising could not afford. The three PR methods you need to know are:

  • Product placement — getting the product into a TV show, film, video or prominent social media post without it being explicitly labelled as an advert. A small candle-maker whose candles appear in a popular lifestyle blogger’s video benefits from organic exposure.
  • Celebrity endorsement — a well-known individual publicly recommends or uses the product. For a start-up, this might mean a local sports personality or community figure using and sharing the product on their social channels rather than a national celebrity deal.
  • Press releases — a written statement sent to journalists, local newspapers, bloggers or radio stations announcing something newsworthy about the business — a launch, a charity partnership, a milestone or an award. If picked up by the media, it generates free coverage.

Advertising is guaranteed to appear — the business pays and the advert runs. PR coverage is not guaranteed: a press release may be ignored, a celebrity endorsement may receive backlash, or a product placement may go unnoticed. However, when PR works, it tends to be more credible than advertising because it appears to come from a neutral source (a journalist, a blogger, a local figure) rather than from the business itself. For a small start-up on a limited budget, a well-timed press release about a local award or community project can generate the same reach as a paid advert at zero cost.
lessons.exam_tip_html: The most common error on advertising questions is treating “promotion” and “advertising” as the same thing — advertising is one type of promotion, not the whole category. Make sure you know and can distinguish all seven non-digital mediums including TV adverts (added in 2025, which means early exam series are likely to test this specifically). For social media questions, always clarify whether you are describing a business-generated post (controlled by the business) or a third-party-generated post (created by customers or influencers) — the specification treats these as separate and an examiner will expect the distinction. On 6-mark “Analyse” questions about promotional choices, embed the scenario business name and a specific detail (budget, product, target audience) in your first sentence, then build your analytical chains from there. Generic answers that apply equally to any business will stall below the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Advertising mediums include seven non-digital types (leaflets, newspapers, magazines, radio, billboards, cinema, TV adverts) and seven digital types (social media, social networks, websites, online banners, SMS, podcasts, vlogs). Social media posts split into business-generated (controlled by the business) and third-party-generated (by customers or influencers).
  • The seven sales promotion techniques are discounts, competitions, BOGOF, point of sale, free gifts, loyalty schemes and sponsorship. These are short-term tactics designed to drive an immediate purchase decision.
  • Public relations (PR) builds a positive reputation through unpaid media coverage. The three PR methods are product placement, celebrity endorsement and press releases. PR is generally lower cost than advertising but less predictable — coverage is earned, not guaranteed.

practice_questions.text:
Yarrow & Stem is a small Ltd company in Hereford run by two founders, selling wildflower seed packets. They want to boost sales quickly before the spring planting season and have a promotional budget of £400. They are considering either a BOGOF offer or a local radio advertising campaign.

Justify which promotional option you would recommend to Yarrow & Stem.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A clear recommendation is made and developed with specific reference to the scenario (seasonal urgency, £400 budget, wildflower seed packets, small Ltd). The recommended option's advantages are explained with good reason chains, and at least one drawback of the recommended option or advantage of the alternative is acknowledged. The justification is grounded in the specific context — for example, BOGOF directly incentivises immediate purchase (important before spring), costs no cash outlay beyond reduced margin, and is easy to implement on a £400 budget; alternatively, radio can reach a local audience quickly and generate awareness beyond existing customers, but £400 may be insufficient for a campaign with meaningful reach. A developed conclusion adds a new evaluative point — for example, that BOGOF is the better choice because Yarrow & Stem needs to sell existing stock quickly rather than build long-term awareness.

Secure (3–4 marks): A clear recommendation with developed reasoning that uses some scenario detail. At least one reason chain is clear. Some acknowledgement of trade-offs.

Developing (2 marks): A preference is stated with basic reasoning. Limited engagement with the specific scenario.

Emerging (1 mark): A preference is stated with little or no supporting reasoning.

practice_questions.text:
Greybridge Brew Co is a small partnership in Sheffield producing craft coffee. The founders, Marcus and Amara, are deciding between two promotional approaches:

Option A: Invest £600 in a TV advert on a regional channel to reach a broad local audience.
Option B: Invite a popular local food blogger with 18,000 followers to try the coffee and write a review.

Analyse how each option might help Greybridge Brew Co achieve its promotional objectives.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Analyses both options with clear analytical chains and specific reference to the scenario. For Option A (TV advert): strong visual impact and broad reach, but expensive for a small partnership (£600 may buy limited airtime on regional TV); the advert is controlled by the business but is obviously promotional, which may not build the same trust as editorial coverage. For Option B (blogger review): a third-party-generated post that is perceived as independent and trustworthy by the blogger's 18,000 followers; it may cost nothing or a very small fee (product sample), meaning more of the promotional budget is preserved; however, the business cannot control what the blogger writes and a neutral or negative review could damage reputation. Explores the trade-offs explicitly and reaches a supported analytical conclusion.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies at least one advantage of each option with some analytical development. Some reference to the scenario.

Developing (2 marks): Describes the two options without clear analytical chains or scenario engagement.

Emerging (1 mark): Names one or both options with minimal analysis.

practice_questions.text:
Bluebell Bath Co is a sole trader in Norwich making luxury bath products. The owner, Faye, wants to build a loyal customer base and is considering introducing a loyalty scheme.

Discuss whether a loyalty scheme is likely to be the most effective sales promotion technique for Bluebell Bath Co.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9 marks): Develops both sides of the argument with clear reasoning and specific application to the scenario (luxury bath products, sole trader, building a loyal customer base). In favour: a loyalty scheme rewards repeat purchase directly, which aligns with Faye's objective of building a loyal base; it encourages customers to return rather than switching to a competitor for a lower-priced alternative; for a small business, knowing customers will return provides a more stable revenue base. Against: a loyalty scheme alone does not attract new customers — if awareness is low, there is nobody to retain; the administrative cost of running a points or stamp scheme may be significant for a sole trader with no support staff; other techniques such as a BOGOF on a bestselling product or a competition on social media might generate more immediate buzz and new customer acquisition. Evaluative conclusion adds new thinking — for example, that loyalty schemes work best once a customer base already exists, so Faye should focus first on advertising or PR to attract new customers, then introduce a loyalty scheme to retain them.

Secure (5–7 marks): Addresses both sides with some development and scenario reference. Conclusion is present.

Developing (3–4 marks): Identifies advantages or disadvantages of a loyalty scheme with limited balance or scenario application.

Emerging (1–2 marks): States a view with little justification or scenario engagement.

lessons.title: Selling Channels and the Product Lifecycle
lessons.description: How and where a start-up sells, plus the five lifecycle stages and extension strategies.
lessons.content_html:
How Does a Start-Up Reach Its Customers?

Once a business has developed its product, it must decide how customers will be able to buy it. These routes to the customer are called selling channels. Choosing the right channel shapes the price, the customer experience and the cost structure of the business — so it is one of the most practical decisions a new entrepreneur makes.

Broadly speaking, selling channels split into two types: physical channels and digital channels. A start-up may use just one or a combination of both.

Physical Selling Channels

Physical channels involve the customer and the seller meeting in person or collecting the product from a fixed location. Common physical channels for a small start-up include:

  • A shop or market stall — the entrepreneur rents or owns a space where customers can browse and buy. This suits products customers want to touch or try before buying, such as handmade jewellery or fresh produce.
  • Face-to-face selling — visiting customers directly, as a mobile hairdresser or a trades person would. The personal relationship can build loyalty, but it is time-intensive and limits how many customers can be reached.

Physical channels tend to have higher overhead costs (rent, staff, fixtures) but can create a stronger customer experience, particularly where trust or personal service matters.

Digital Selling Channels

Digital channels allow a business to sell to customers anywhere, at any time, without the overhead of a physical premises. For many new start-ups, digital channels are the most affordable way to reach a large audience quickly. Key digital channels include:

E-commerce through a business’s own website gives the entrepreneur full control over branding, pricing and the customer experience. Running costs are lower than a physical shop, and the business can serve customers 24 hours a day. The challenge for a new start-up is driving traffic to the site — without an established reputation, customers may not find it.

Social media platforms now include built-in shopping features where sellers can list and sell products directly to followers. This is a fast, low-cost way for a new business to reach an audience that already follows the brand. Online auction platforms allow businesses to reach a wider audience by listing items in a competitive bidding environment, which can be useful when selling unique or limited-run products. Both routes give access to an existing pool of buyers without requiring the business to build its own customer base from scratch.

Some businesses sell products that exist entirely online — music files, software, digital art, e-books or online courses. These can be delivered instantly to the customer with no physical handling costs, no postage and no stock to manage. Profit margins on digital downloads are typically very high once the product has been created, because the same product can be sold to thousands of customers with no additional production cost.

Key Fact

Physical channels (shop, market stall, face-to-face) suit products that customers want to handle or where personal service matters. Digital channels (e-commerce website, social media marketplace, online auctions, downloads) reduce overheads and extend geographic reach. Most start-ups combine both to maximise sales opportunities.

The Product Lifecycle

Every product, from the day it is conceived to the day it is withdrawn from sale, passes through a series of recognisable stages. This pattern is called the product lifecycle. Understanding which stage a product is at helps a business decide how to price it, how much to spend on promotion, and whether to invest in keeping it alive or launch something new.

The five stages are: development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Sales data tells the story — in an exam, you may be asked to look at a table or graph of sales figures and identify which stage a product is in. You will not be asked to draw the lifecycle curve itself.

During development, the product does not yet exist in a form ready for sale. The business is spending money on research, design and testing but earning nothing. Cash flow is negative and the risk is high — the product may never reach the market.

At introduction, the product launches. Sales begin but are usually low because awareness is limited. Promotional spend is high to build recognition. The business is still likely to be making a loss at this stage. Imagine Floret Skincare, a new Leeds-based soap brand launching its first range — it has costs (ingredients, packaging, marketing) but its first sales are modest.

In the growth stage, sales rise rapidly as the product becomes better known. The business moves into profit. Competitors begin to notice and may enter the market with similar products. Floret Skincare would be expanding its stockists and launching new scents.

At maturity, sales reach their peak and stabilise. This is typically the most profitable stage — most customers in the target market know about the product and competition is fierce. Businesses compete on quality, price and promotion rather than novelty. Branded everyday items like well-known shampoo ranges or breakfast cereals spend years in maturity.

Sales fall consistently during decline. This may happen because consumer tastes change, new technology makes the product obsolete, or a stronger competitor takes market share. A DVD rental service is a well-known example of a business whose core product went into decline as streaming overtook it. At this point the business must decide: withdraw the product, cut costs to serve a small loyal niche, or invest in an extension strategy.

Key Fact

The five stages of the product lifecycle are: development (no sales, spending on creation), introduction (low sales, high promotion, likely a loss), growth (rising sales, rising profit), maturity (peak sales, maximum profit, heavy competition) and decline (falling sales and profit). In an exam, use the shape of sales data to identify the stage.

Extension Strategies

A business rarely wants to withdraw a product once it has built a loyal customer base. Extension strategies are deliberately planned actions to extend the life of a product. They are typically applied during maturity (to prevent decline) or at the start of decline (to reverse it). Common extension strategies include:

  • Increased advertising — a fresh campaign targets existing customers or reaches a new audience, rebuilding awareness and demand.
  • Price reductions — lowering the price attracts customers who were previously put off by the cost, expanding the pool of buyers.
  • Adding value — including extra features, a longer warranty, or bundling with a complementary product makes the offer more attractive without fundamentally redesigning it.
  • New packaging — a refreshed look modernises the product’s appearance without changing what is inside, attracting customers who had lost interest.
  • Entering new markets — selling to a different customer group (younger buyers, a different income segment) or expanding geographically into overseas markets can unlock entirely new revenue streams.

Extension strategies cost money, so the entrepreneur must weigh whether the likely boost in revenue is worth the investment. If the product is genuinely obsolete — no longer wanted by any segment — even a large promotional budget will not revive it. However, for a product with genuine appeal, a well-timed strategy can add years of profitable sales and delay the need to develop something entirely new.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Explain question about selling channels, avoid describing just one channel. Explain why a specific channel suits the start-up in the question — for example, linking a social media marketplace to a young target audience or low start-up budget. That application is what lifts an answer from Developing to Secure. For questions about the product lifecycle, use the sales data provided to name the stage first, then analyse what that stage means for the business’s decisions (pricing, promotion, investment). The examiner’s top complaint is generic answers that could apply to any business. This lesson feeds directly into extended-response evaluation questions on the marketing mix, which account for a significant share of the written exam — practise linking channel choice and lifecycle stage to the full marketing mix.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Selling channels are how a business reaches its customers — physical channels (shops, face-to-face) suit personal or tactile products; digital channels (e-commerce, social media, downloads) reduce costs and extend reach.
  • The five product lifecycle stages are development, introduction, growth, maturity and decline. Each stage has a different sales level, profitability and set of marketing priorities. In an exam you identify the stage from sales data — you will not be asked to draw the curve.
  • Extension strategies — increased advertising, price reductions, adding value, new packaging and entering new markets — can delay or reverse decline, but only if the cost is justified by the expected boost in revenue.

lessons.title: Pricing a Product
lessons.description: Four factors that shape your price and the four pricing strategies every start-up needs to know.
lessons.content_html:
Why Pricing Is One of the Most Important Decisions a Start-Up Makes

Getting the price right matters enormously for a new business. Set it too high and customers will go elsewhere. Set it too low and the business will not cover its costs, let alone make a profit. Price is also a signal — customers make judgements about quality based on what something costs. A handmade ceramic vase priced at an extremely low level may feel untrustworthy, while the same vase priced confidently communicates craft and care.

Before choosing a pricing strategy, an entrepreneur should think carefully about four key factors that shape the decision.

Four Factors That Influence Pricing

The more money a target customer earns, the more they are likely to be willing to spend on a product. A business selling to higher-income customers can justify a premium price and use that price to signal quality and exclusivity. A business selling to lower-income customers needs to keep the price accessible — if the price feels out of reach, customers will walk away regardless of how good the product is.

When customers can easily compare prices — as they can on almost any digital channel — charging significantly more than competitors is risky unless the business can clearly justify the difference. A new coffee shop opening near several established competitors must think about what local customers currently pay, because pricing dramatically higher will deter potential customers who have other options.

A business must always know what it costs to make or source each unit. If the price does not cover those costs, every sale generates a loss. This does not mean the price is purely determined by cost — but cost sets a floor below which the business cannot sustainably trade. If production costs rise (for instance, the price of raw materials increases), the business faces a difficult choice: absorb the cost, reduce profit margins, or pass it on to customers through a price rise.

The appropriate price changes as the product moves through its lifecycle. At introduction, a brand-new product with no competition may be able to sustain a high price because early adopters will pay a premium. As the product matures and more competitors enter, the business may need to review its price to stay competitive. At decline, a price reduction may be used as an extension strategy to attract price-sensitive customers who were previously put off.

Key Fact

Four factors influence a business’s pricing decision: income levels of target customers (determines what they can afford), competitor prices (sets a reference point customers will use), cost of production (the floor below which the business makes a loss) and stage of the product lifecycle (shapes how much premium or discount the market will accept).

The Four Pricing Strategies

A pricing strategy is the deliberate approach a business takes to pricing — not just picking a number, but choosing a method that fits the product, the customer and the competition. There are four strategies that a start-up needs to know.

Competitive pricing means pricing in line with rivals. This is common in markets where products are broadly similar and customers will compare prices before buying — think of local takeaway menus or supermarket own-brand products. The advantage is that the business does not risk losing customers purely on price. The risk is that margins can be thin, especially if a price war develops where all competitors keep cutting.

Psychological pricing exploits the way customers perceive numbers. A product priced just below a round number feels significantly cheaper, even though the actual difference is small. A craft gin bottle presented at a price just below a round-number threshold feels like a bargain compared with the same bottle at the round number, even though the difference is minor. This strategy suits consumer goods where the buying decision is partly emotional.

Price skimming involves setting a high price at launch and reducing it over time. It works when the product is genuinely new, in demand, and has no close competition. Early adopters — customers who want to be first — are willing to pay a premium for exclusivity. As the novelty fades and competitors appear, the price is lowered to reach a broader market. This strategy suits innovative or distinctive products rather than everyday commodities.

Penetration pricing does the opposite: the launch price is deliberately low to attract customers away from established competitors and build market share fast. The business accepts lower — or even negative — margins initially, betting that once customers are loyal they will stay even if the price rises. This suits new entrants to a competitive market where the established players have higher prices.

Key Fact

The four pricing strategies are: competitive (match rivals to avoid losing on price), psychological (price just below a round number to feel like a bargain), skimming (high at launch to maximise early revenue, then reduce) and penetration (low at launch to win market share, then raise). No single strategy is always best — the right choice depends on the product, the market and the competition.

Choosing the Right Strategy

The four influencing factors and the four strategies work together. Consider Millbrook Candle Co., a new small candle start-up in Cardiff. Its customers are mid-income gift buyers. Its costs are modest. There are several established candle brands in the same price bracket. A skimming strategy would struggle here because the product is not genuinely new or scarce. A penetration strategy might win customers initially but thin margins on a low-volume product could cause cash flow problems. Competitive pricing — matching the established brands while using psychological pricing on individual lines — would be a sensible starting point, giving the business a foothold without a price war.

Remember: the spec states that worked pricing examples should be about the type of strategy chosen and why, not about calculating a specific price figure. You will not be asked to work out a price in a formula — you will be asked to recommend and justify a strategy based on the context given.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Explain or 6-mark Analyse question on pricing, always connect your chosen strategy to the specific start-up in the question — name its product, its customer type, or its competitive situation. A generic answer describing what penetration pricing is without linking it to why it suits this business will stall in the Developing tier. For 6-mark Justify questions, the command word “justify” requires good reasons for your recommendation, not just a description. Build a reason chain using “because” and “this means that” to connect strategy to business outcome. This lesson also feeds into the extended-response evaluation question on the marketing mix, which always appears in the written exam — pricing strategy is one of the four Ps and must work alongside product, place and promotion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Pricing decisions are shaped by four factors: income levels of target customers, competitor prices, cost of production and the stage of the product lifecycle.
  • The four pricing strategies are competitive (match rivals), psychological (price just below a round number), skimming (high launch price then reduce) and penetration (low launch price to build share). The right choice depends on the product, market and competitive context.
  • In exam questions, justify your recommended strategy with reason chains linked to the scenario — do not just define the strategy. The extended-response evaluation question on the marketing mix rewards answers that show how pricing connects to the other three Ps.

lessons.content_html:
Choosing a Legal Structure

When someone starts a business, one of the first decisions they face is how the business will be legally structured. This is not just administrative paperwork — the chosen structure determines who bears the financial risk, who controls the business, how profits are shared and how much it costs to set up. Getting it wrong can be costly later, so most entrepreneurs think carefully about structure from the start.

The most important concept that runs through all ownership types is unlimited liability. Under unlimited liability, the law treats the owner and the business as the same entity. If the business cannot pay its debts, the owner must pay them from their personal assets — including savings, a car or even a home. This is the greatest financial risk of certain ownership structures.

The opposite is limited liability. Under limited liability, the law treats the business as a separate legal entity from its owners. If the business fails, shareholders only lose what they put in — their personal possessions are safe. This protection makes limited liability structures attractive for any entrepreneur who is investing significant money or taking on meaningful risk.

Key Fact

Unlimited liability — a sole trader and general partners in a standard partnership are personally responsible for all business debts. Limited liability — shareholders in a private limited company (Ltd) and members of a limited liability partnership (LLP) can only lose what they invested. Examiners specifically test whether students know which structure gives which protection — writing “limited responsibility” instead of “limited liability” will cost marks.

The Four Ownership Types (Plus Franchise)

A sole trader is the simplest form of business ownership. There is no formal registration process beyond informing tax authorities. The owner makes all decisions, keeps all the profit after tax and has complete control. This suits independent tradespeople, personal trainers, freelancers and market traders who want flexibility and minimal administration.

The main disadvantages are unlimited liability — every business debt is a personal debt — and limited access to finance, since banks see sole traders as higher risk. If the owner becomes ill or is absent, the business may stop completely. There is also no one to share the workload or contribute complementary skills.

A partnership allows two or more people to go into business together, pooling their skills, experience and start-up capital. A furniture designer and a skilled carpenter, for example, might form a partnership that combines creative and craft expertise neither has alone. Partners share the workload, which can help a business grow faster than a sole trader could manage.

However, standard partners share unlimited liability. If one partner makes a poor business decision that creates a large debt, all partners are personally responsible — even if they had no involvement in that decision. A formal written partnership agreement, setting out each person’s role, decision-making rights and profit share, is strongly recommended to reduce disputes.

A limited liability partnership (LLP) is a variation that gives members the flexibility of a partnership while providing limited liability. This means members’ personal assets are protected if the business cannot pay its debts. LLPs are more common in professional services — law firms and accountancy practices, for example — but are an option available to any start-up that wants the combined skills of a partnership with the financial protection of limited liability.

A private limited company (Ltd) is legally separate from its owners. Shareholders invest in the company and have limited liability — they can only lose the money they put in. This structure requires formal registration with Companies House, and annual accounts are filed publicly. The administration is more complex and costly than a sole trader or partnership.

The advantages are significant: limited liability protects investors, capital can be raised by selling shares to trusted individuals, and the business continues to exist even if a founder leaves or dies. Shares in a private limited company cannot be sold on a stock exchange — they can only be transferred to buyers the existing shareholders approve. This keeps control within a trusted group, which many small business founders prefer.

A franchise is not a legal ownership structure in the same way as sole trader or Ltd — it describes a business operating model. A franchisee buys the right to trade under an established brand and follow a proven system. The advantage is significantly lower risk than starting from scratch: the brand is known, the product or service is tested, and the franchisor provides training and support.

The costs are real, however. The franchisee pays an upfront fee and ongoing royalties — typically a percentage of revenue — to the franchisor. They must follow the franchisor’s rules on pricing, branding and operations. This means the franchisee has far less independence than a sole trader or partner. For someone who wants to run their own business but values the security of a proven model, a franchise can be an attractive route into enterprise.

Key Fact

Sole trader: one owner, unlimited liability, full control, easy to set up. Partnership: shared skills and capital, unlimited liability, risk of disagreement. LLP: partnership flexibility, limited liability for members. Private limited company (Ltd): limited liability, separate legal entity, more administration. Franchise: proven model, lower risk, but less independence and ongoing royalty costs.

Six Sources of Start-Up Capital

Whatever structure a new business adopts, it needs money to get started. This money — called capital — can come from several sources. There are six sources to know.

  • Own savings — using personal savings avoids debt and interest costs. The entrepreneur keeps full control and all future profit. The risk is personal — if the business fails, the savings are lost.
  • Friends and family — money from people close to the entrepreneur can come as a gift (with no repayment obligation) or as an informal loan. This is often faster and easier to arrange than bank finance, but mixing money and personal relationships can create tension if the business struggles.
  • Loans — a bank or financial institution lends a fixed sum that must be repaid with interest over an agreed period. A loan provides a lump sum without giving away ownership of the business, but the obligation to make repayments continues even if sales are low. Note: the loan repayment itself is not classed as a business cost — only the interest on the loan is a cost.
  • Crowdfunding — the entrepreneur pitches the idea on an online platform and many individuals each contribute a small amount. In return, backers may receive an early product, a reward, or (in equity crowdfunding) a small share of the business. Crowdfunding can also generate publicity and test whether there is genuine demand before the product is made.
  • Grants — government bodies, local authorities and some other organisations offer grants to businesses that meet certain criteria, such as being in a specific industry or location. Unlike loans, grants do not have to be repaid, but they are competitive, often come with conditions on how the money is spent, and are not guaranteed.
  • Business angels — wealthy private investors who provide capital in exchange for a share of the business and often an active role as a mentor or advisor. A business angel brings not just money but contacts, experience and guidance. The entrepreneur gives up some ownership and must share future profits and decision-making authority.

Choosing the right source depends on how much capital is needed, how quickly it is needed, how much control the entrepreneur is willing to give up and what obligations come with the money.
lessons.exam_tip_html: On a 4-mark Explain question about limited or unlimited liability, one fully developed point is worth more than two rushed ones. Use the structure: what the term means — what it means specifically for the business in the question — what the practical consequence is for the owner. A very common error is writing “limited responsibility” instead of “limited liability”, or claiming that a sole trader’s business assets are protected. Neither will earn marks. For 6-mark Analyse or 9-mark Discuss questions about ownership structure or finance sources, always embed a detail from the case-study scenario rather than writing a generic textbook definition — examiner reports consistently identify lack of application as the main barrier to reaching the Secure and Mastering tiers.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sole traders and standard partners have unlimited liability — personal assets are at risk. Shareholders in an Ltd and members of an LLP have limited liability — personal assets are protected. Using “limited responsibility” instead of “limited liability” is a mark-losing error.
  • The four ownership types are sole trader (full control, unlimited liability), partnership (shared skills, unlimited liability), LLP (partnership flexibility plus limited liability) and private limited company (limited liability, separate legal entity). A franchise is a different kind of start-up model: lower risk but less independence and ongoing royalty costs.
  • The six sources of start-up capital are: own savings, friends and family (gift or loan), loans (interest is a cost; repayment is not), crowdfunding, grants and business angels. Each has trade-offs between cost, control and obligation.

lessons.title: Support for an Enterprise
lessons.description: Where new business owners go for help — finance, professional, community and government support.
lessons.content_html:
Why Do New Business Owners Need Support?

Starting a business is rarely a solo journey. Most new entrepreneurs encounter questions they cannot answer alone — how to manage accounts, whether a contract is legally sound, how to apply for funding, or how to find other local businesses to learn from. Knowing where to find the right help, at the right moment, can be the difference between a business that survives its first year and one that fails through avoidable mistakes.

The kind of support a start-up needs changes at different stages. In the early days, the focus is often on finance and legal structure. Later, it might be about finding customers or managing staff. The key skill — and what this lesson explores — is matching the right type of support to the right problem.

Sources of Support

There are several different categories of support available to a new business. Some provide money, some provide expertise, some provide community and connections, and some provide practical services. A smart entrepreneur draws on more than one.

A bank can provide a range of financial products to a new business: loans to fund start-up costs, business current accounts for day-to-day transactions, and access to financial advice. Banks typically want evidence that the business has a credible plan and a realistic chance of repaying any money borrowed. For a brand-new business with no trading history, getting finance from a bank can be challenging — which is why many entrepreneurs combine bank support with other sources.

A business angel is a private investor who provides capital in exchange for a share of the business and often a seat at the table as a mentor or advisor. Beyond the money itself, a business angel typically brings industry experience, a network of useful contacts, and a genuine stake in seeing the business succeed. This can be especially valuable for a start-up whose founder has a great idea but limited business experience.

The government provides a range of support for new businesses through national schemes and programmes. This can include grants (money that does not need to be repaid), information and guidance on starting up, and training or mentoring schemes. Government support is typically targeted at specific types of business, industries or locations, so a new enterprise must check whether it qualifies before applying.

A local council enterprise department often offers support that is specifically tailored to businesses in that area. This might include help with finding suitable premises, advice on local business rates, introductions to other local businesses, and information about area-specific grants or regeneration funding. Local support tends to be more accessible for a brand-new small business than national programmes, which may be more competitive.

An accountant helps a new business keep on top of its finances. For a start-up, this typically includes setting up bookkeeping systems, preparing tax returns, making sure the business meets its legal obligations to report income, and advising on whether the business is generating profit or heading towards difficulty. Many sole traders and small partnerships use an accountant even if they could manage some of these tasks themselves, simply because professional financial management reduces costly errors.

A solicitor is a legal expert. A new business may need a solicitor to draft or review contracts, register a trademark, advise on the legal structure of a partnership or company, or handle any dispute with a supplier or customer. Legal mistakes are often expensive — a poorly written contract, for example, could leave the business without recourse if a major customer refuses to pay. Using a solicitor early to set up the right legal foundations is often cheaper than dealing with problems later.

Friends and family can be a source of informal support that goes well beyond money. A family member with marketing experience might help with social media. A friend who has set up their own business might share practical advice about what worked and what did not. This informal network is often the first port of call for a new entrepreneur and should not be underestimated.

The Chamber of Commerce is a membership organisation for local businesses. Joining gives access to networking events where entrepreneurs can meet potential customers, suppliers and partners. The Chamber often provides training sessions, business advice workshops and a collective voice to advocate for local business interests to the council or government. For a new start-up looking to build its local network quickly, the Chamber of Commerce can be a genuinely practical resource.

Charitable organisations exist in most parts of the UK to support new or struggling businesses, particularly those run by people from disadvantaged backgrounds or those operating in areas of economic need. Charitable support might include free or subsidised business mentoring, access to shared workspace, help with writing a business plan, or connections to grant funding. Unlike banks, charities are not looking for a financial return, so the support they provide is often more accessible for an early-stage business that has not yet proven its viability.

Key Fact

Eight sources of support for a new enterprise: bank (loans, accounts, financial advice), business angel (capital plus mentoring and contacts), government (grants and guidance schemes), local council enterprise department (local premises, rates and area-specific funding), accountant (financial management and tax), solicitor (contracts and legal structure), friends and family (informal advice and support), Chamber of Commerce (networking and training), charities (mentoring and accessible support for early-stage businesses).

Choosing the Right Support

The analytical skill that examiners reward is not just listing sources of support — it is matching the right support to the right situation. Consider three different entrepreneurs:

  • Kezia is starting a food business but has no experience of bookkeeping or tax returns. An accountant is the most directly useful professional for her at this stage, before mistakes accumulate.
  • Marcus is a young entrepreneur with a strong product idea but no industry contacts and limited business experience. A business angel would provide both capital and the mentoring he needs to avoid common pitfalls — at the cost of giving up some ownership.
  • Priya wants to rent a workshop in her town and is looking for local grants. A local council enterprise department is the most targeted starting point, since they hold information about local premises and area-specific funding that national sources would not know about.

In each case, the most appropriate source of support depends on the specific challenge the entrepreneur is facing. A high-mark answer in an exam will always connect the type of support to the entrepreneur’s situation explicitly.

The R067 spec assesses your ability to match support to a specific situation. Identify the entrepreneur's biggest current problem first (cash, legal, premises, expertise), then pick the support source that solves that exact problem.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For a 4-mark Explain question on sources of support, the common mistake is listing lots of sources without explaining why any of them suit the business in the question. Pick one or two sources and build a reason chain: what this source provides — why that is relevant to the specific entrepreneur’s challenge — what the consequence is for the business. For a 6-mark Analyse question, develop at least two well-connected points that each link a specific source of support to the business context. Generic answers that could describe any start-up stall in the Developing tier. Examiner reports consistently identify application to the scenario as the key discriminator on medium and extended-mark questions — use the business name, the product, the location or the owner’s background to embed your analysis.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Sources of support for a new enterprise include finance providers (bank, business angel), government and local council, professional advisors (accountant, solicitor), community and network support (friends, family, Chamber of Commerce) and charitable organisations.
  • Different sources suit different situations: banks and business angels help with capital; accountants and solicitors prevent costly legal and financial errors; local councils and charities offer accessible support for early-stage businesses.
  • In exam questions, the skill is matching the right support to the specific entrepreneur’s challenge — always link your answer to the details of the scenario rather than listing all support sources.
